figures.caption: Fig. 1 (a) Representative charge and discharge proﬁles of Li–In|b-Li3PS4|NCM-811+b-Li3PS4 cells applying diﬀerent upper cut-oﬀvoltages. The SSBs are cycled between 2.7 V (lower boundary) and 4.0 V, 4.3 V, 4.6 V or 5.0 V vs. Li+/Li, respectively (a–d). The bold curves show the ﬁrst charge and discharge. The grey arrows denote the 2nd, 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th and 25th cycle (from right to left). The current density for all cycles corresponds to 0.1C (214 mA cm2).

Fig. 2 (a) Discharge capacities of Li–In|b-Li3PS4|NCM-811+b-Li3PS4 cells charged to cut-oﬀvoltages of 4.0 V, 4.3 V, 4.6 V and 5.0 V (vs. Li+/ Li), respectively. The ﬁrst cycle discharge capacity is always lower than the following ones. The current density was 214 mA cm2, which corresponds to 0.1C for the cell charged to 4.3 V. (b) Evolution of the average charging voltage. The overvoltage increases during the ﬁrst battery cycles and increases with higher cut-oﬀvoltages.

Fig. 3 Nyquist plots of the Li–In|b-Li3PS4|NCM-811+b-Li3PS4 cells cycled at 214 mA cm2 to diﬀerent upper voltage limitations between 4.0 V and 5.0 V (a–d). Spectra recorded in the discharged state after 25 cycles and a 24 hour OCV period. Open circles indicate the measured data, and solid lines represent the resulting ﬁt using an equivalent circuit of (RQ)(RQ)(RQ)(RQ). The cathode interfacial resistance is highlighted in grey. These data show that the cathode/solid electrolyte impedance is severely growing when charging occurs at higher potentials.

Fig. 4 (a) Evolution of Rcathode/SE upon cycling for Li–In|b-Li3PS4|NCM-811+b-Li3PS4 batteries charged to diﬀerent upper cut-oﬀvoltages between 4.0 V and 5.0 V (a–d). The resistance was evaluated from EIS measurements, recorded after each charge and discharge process. Filled boxes represent the charged and open boxes the discharged state. At 4.0 V a formation step reduces the interfacial resistance during the ﬁrst few cycles. This formation step is less obvious when charging to higher cut-oﬀvoltages. The resistance increase by oxidative decomposition detrimentally mitigates the resistance drop from the surface formation. The diﬀerence in the interfacial resistance between the charged and discharged states during cycling suggests a partially reversible redox process that limits ion conduction at the interface.

Fig. 5 Waterfall plots of the S 2p signal vs. etching time after 25 cycles at 0.1C for the diﬀerent upper cut-oﬀvoltages (4.0 V to 5.0 V, a–d). Stacked spectra taken after 0 to 16 minutes of etching time are shown as the most signiﬁcant changes are observed within this etching time. Additionally, a spectrum at 40 minutes of etching is provided indicating no further changes upon increased etching time. Exemplary peak de- convolution is shown for the spectra obtained directly at the cathode/CC interface surface without etching (surface ¼ 0 min). Blue peaks are attributed to equivalent Pd+–Sd bonds (161.4 eV). Green peaks are correlated with bridged P–[S]n–P binding environments (162.7 eV). The orange signals are assigned to more oxidized sulfur such as in S0 (163.5 eV). Clearly, the thiophosphate SE is oxidized at the interface to the CC.

Fig. 6 (a) Quantiﬁcation of the cathode interface at the current collector from XPS S 2p spectra at diﬀerent etching times and for diﬀerent upper cut-oﬀvoltages. Cathodes were cycled 25 times at diﬀerent cut-oﬀvoltages ranging from 4.0 V to 5.0 V (a–d) and were measured in the discharged state. The current collector is illustrated in grey and the thickness of the cathode electrolyte interphase region (at the current collector) is only estimated. The checkered blue area represents the fraction of sulfur atoms in PS4 3 tetrahedra, which gives a good measure of the SE oxidation at the CC interface. The oxidized species correlated with bridging P–S–P and S–S type environments are lower in the phase fraction, and their fractions decrease with increasing etching time. figures.caption: Fig. 8 Reaction scheme for the proposed redox reactions of Li3PS4. During oxidation, two Li3PS4 units can merge to a corner- or edge-sharing species, Li4P2S8 and Li4P2S7 or Li2P2S6, respectively. Lithium ions are transferred to the counter electrode and elemental sulfur is accumulated at the positive electrode. During reduction the process is reversed, the original Li3PS4 structure is expected to be formed again. However, further reduction to Li4P2S6 under Li2S subtraction is likely. For each species only a single tautomeric structure is shown.
